synopsis: Graphics-card choice strongly affects sensor-simulation speed and scene capacity: ray-tracing cores accelerate camera, lidar and radar calculations, while VRAM limits scene size; most named cards are NVIDIA models because the reviewed simulators depend on NVIDIA ray-tracing libraries [f16191, f16205, f16206, f16192]. CARLA UE5 requires at least an NVIDIA RTX 3000-series GPU with 16 GB VRAM, alongside Ubuntu 22.04 or Windows 11 and 130 GB of disk; the RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell offers 96 GB of memory, but its server prices were not found [f8469, f8852, f16198]. The booklet's 2026 cloud prices include AWS G6e with L40S GPUs at USD 1.861–30.131 per hour on demand in us-east-1, and Google g2-standard-32 with one L4 at about USD 1.734 per hour; these are generic pay-per-use options, not evidence of off-road suitability [f9258, f9260, f9257, f9259]. Illustrative performance figures include RadaRays at 7.8–18.8 milliseconds per radar image on an RTX 2070 Super versus 25.8–78.5 milliseconds on a desktop CPU, SplatAD scene training in about one hour on an A100, and weather editing at 20.52 seconds per image on an A40 [f16196, f16200, f16201]. No neutral, controlled cross-vendor benchmark was found, and reported multi-sensor frame-rate losses mean every candidate must be timed with the program's own machine geometry and sensors; Chrono's NVIDIA requirement is explicitly a dependency risk rather than a recommendation [f16208, f16207, f16209, f16193].
